# JavaScript code built from HTTP request data (Node.js)

`qualor:js/code-injection` · Issue · Severity: High · [CWE-94](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/94.html), [CWE-95](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/95.html) · OWASP Top 10: [A05:2025 Injection](https://top10.owasp.org/2025/A05_2025-Injection/), [A03:2021 Injection](https://top10.owasp.org/2021/A03_2021-Injection/)

## What it finds

<!-- begin: what-it-finds -->
HTTP request data that is run as JavaScript code on the server:

- `eval()`, also called indirectly (`(0, eval)(x)`, `globalThis.eval(x)`);
- the `Function` constructor, with or without `new` (every argument is code);
- `node:vm`: `runInNewContext`, `runInContext`, `runInThisContext`, `compileFunction`,
  `new vm.Script` and `new vm.SourceTextModule`.

Request data is followed in Express, Fastify, Next.js route handlers and Node's `http` servers.
<!-- end: what-it-finds -->

## Why it matters

<!-- begin: why-it-matters -->
Code built from request data runs with all the rights of the server process: a client can read
environment variables and files, open connections or start processes. The Node.js documentation
states that `node:vm` is not a security mechanism, so running the code in a new context does not
help either.
<!-- end: why-it-matters -->

## Example

<!-- begin: example -->
**Noncompliant:** a list of ids sent by the client is turned into a value with `eval()`.

```javascript
const express = require('express');

const app = express();

app.get('/report', (req, res) => {
  const ids = eval(req.query.ids);
  res.json({ count: ids.length });
});
```

**Compliant:** the text is parsed as JSON, which yields only data.

```javascript
const express = require('express');

const app = express();

app.get('/report', (req, res) => {
  const ids = JSON.parse(req.query.ids);
  res.json({ count: ids.length });
});
```
<!-- end: example -->

## How to fix

<!-- begin: how-to-fix -->
- Do not build code from request data. To turn text into data, use `JSON.parse()`.
- Pass request values to fixed code as arguments, or as context values of a fixed `vm` script.
- For formulas or filters that users write, use an expression parser that cannot reach
  JavaScript, or pick the code from an allow-list of functions.
<!-- end: how-to-fix -->

## Frameworks and APIs covered

- Express
- Next.js
- Fastify
- Node.js http
- Node.js vm

## Known limits

<!-- begin: known-limits -->
- A check of the code before the call (a regular expression that allows only digits and
  operators) is not recognised: the checked value is still reported.
- An allow-list lookup is recognised only in a table declared `const` in the same file, with
  literal keys and values, that the file never writes to; nested tables, tables from other modules
  and strings with escaped quotes are not, so their lookups are reported.
- Request handlers are recognised by the name of their second parameter (`res`, `response`,
  `reply`, `ctx`, `next`, ...): a handler written as `(request, out)` is not checked, and a
  one-parameter callback passed to `get()`/`post()` after a path is taken for a Fastify handler.
<!-- end: known-limits -->

## Tests

The test files [`rules/js/code/code-injection.js`](../../../rules/js/code/code-injection.js) and [`rules/js/code/code-injection.ts`](../../../rules/js/code/code-injection.ts) hold every case the rule reports or accepts:
lines marked `ruleid:` must be reported and lines marked `ok:` must not. The known limits are
marked `todoruleid:` (missed) and `todook:` (wrongly reported). `npm test` runs them with OpenGrep,
and checks the example above as well.
